title: Mass Spectrometry
description: Ion sources, mass analyzers, tandem MS, and the coupling of MS to GC and LC.
overview: A mass spectrometer weighs ions. It turns the analyte into gas-phase ions, separates them by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) and counts them. The result is a spectrum of ion abundance against m/z, from which the molar mass, the elemental composition, the structure and the amount of the analyte can be found. Mass spectrometry is the most sensitive general-purpose detector in chemistry (attomole amounts) and, coupled to chromatography, the standard tool for identifying and quantifying compounds in complex mixtures.

This chapter treats the instrument in the order of the ions’ path: ionization methods, mass analyzers and their figures of merit, tandem MS, and then the coupling to GC and LC and to ICP for elemental speciation. The interpretation of EI fragmentation patterns of organic molecules (the McLafferty rearrangement, the nitrogen rule) belongs to the chapter on organic spectroscopy, and the ICP source to the chapter on atomic spectroscopy.
objectives: Compare hard and soft ionization: EI, CI, ESI, APCI and MALDI, and choose a source for a given analyte.
Explain how quadrupole, time-of-flight, ion-trap, Orbitrap and FT-ICR analyzers separate ions, and compare resolving power and mass accuracy.
Calculate resolving power and mass accuracy, and decide what resolution is needed to separate two ions.
Explain tandem MS, collision-induced dissociation, and the scan modes of a triple quadrupole (product ion, precursor ion, SRM/MRM).
Describe GC–MS and LC–MS, SIM, ion suppression, and quantitation with isotope-labeled internal standards.
Explain how hyphenated techniques, such as HPLC–ICP–MS, are used for speciation.

sections.title: Ionization methods
body: The ion source decides what kinds of molecules can be analyzed and how much fragmentation the spectrum shows. A hard source gives much fragmentation, with a rich fingerprint but often no molecular ion. A soft source gives mainly the intact molecule, with its mass but little structural information.

Mechanism
Analytes
Ions formed
Notes

Volatile, thermally stable, M < 600 u (GC effluent)

Polar and ionic molecules, from small drugs to proteins (up to MDa)

A heated nebulizer evaporates the solution; a corona discharge ionizes the solvent vapor, which protonates the analyte
Less polar, medium-mass molecules (steroids, lipids, pesticides)

table.caption: Common ionization sources.

body: The molecule M in the vacuum meets an electron of 70 eV: M + e⁻ → M⁺• + 2e⁻. The ionization energy of an organic molecule is only 8–12 eV, so the excess of energy leaves the molecular ion with a high internal energy and it fragments by bond cleavage. 70 eV is chosen because the ionization efficiency is at a maximum and the spectrum varies little with the energy, so a spectrum measured on any instrument is the same, and libraries of more than 300,000 compounds (the NIST library) can be searched for an identification.

In **electrospray**, a solution flows through a metal capillary held at a few kV. The field draws the liquid into a **Taylor cone**, which emits a jet that breaks into charged droplets. A drying gas and heat evaporate the solvent; as a droplet shrinks, the charge density rises until the repulsion overcomes the surface tension (the Rayleigh limit) and the droplet fissions into smaller droplets. Small ions are finally released into the gas phase (the ion evaporation model for small molecules; the charge residue model for large ones). The key practical consequence is that large molecules acquire many charges: a protein of mass M picks up n protons, and appears at m/z = (M + n × 1.00728)/n. Because the m/z values are small (500–2500) even for a protein of 50 kDa, a quadrupole or TOF analyzer can measure it, and the mass is calculated from a series of peaks (deconvolution).

example.title: Charge states of a protein
example.problem: Two adjacent peaks in the ESI spectrum of a protein appear at m/z 1001.0 and 1112.2. Find the charges and the mass.
example.solution: Adjacent charge states differ by one proton. Let the peak at 1112.2 carry n charges and the peak at 1001.0 carry n + 1. Each peak obeys m/z = (M + 1.007n)/n, so M = n(1112.2 − 1.007) = (n+1)(1001.0 − 1.007). So 1111.19n = 999.99(n+1), giving 111.2n = 999.99, n = 8.99 ≈ 9. M = 9 × 1111.19 = 10,000.7 ≈ 10,000 u: the peaks are the [M+10H]¹⁰⁺ at 1001.0 and [M+9H]⁹⁺ at 1112.2.

sections.title: Mass analyzers
body: The analyzer separates the ions by m/z. Its main figures of merit are the mass range, the speed, the **resolving power** R = m/Δm (where Δm is the peak width at half height, FWHM, or two peaks of equal height that are separated by Δm with a valley of 10%), and the **mass accuracy**, the error of the measured mass in ppm: (m_measured − m_true)/m_true × 10⁶.

head: Analyzer
Principle
Resolving power
Mass accuracy
Characteristics
rows: Four rods with RF + DC voltages; only ions of one m/z have a stable path
Robust, cheap, fast scanning; the core of GC–MS and the triple quadrupole. Poor above m/z 4000.
Ions accelerated through a fixed voltage fly down a drift tube; lighter ions arrive first
No upper mass limit; spectrum in microseconds; pulsed sources (MALDI) or orthogonal acceleration (ESI).
Ions are confined in an RF field and ejected by m/z
Can do MSⁿ in time (isolate, fragment, repeat) in one place.
Ions orbit around a central spindle electrode, oscillating axially at a frequency ∝ (z/m)^{1/2}; image current is Fourier-transformed
High resolution and accuracy in a benchtop instrument; the proteomics and metabolomics standard.
Ions in a 7–21 T field circulate at the cyclotron frequency ω = qB/m; the image current is Fourier-transformed
Highest resolution, an expensive superconducting magnet; petroleomics, complex mixtures.

body: In the **quadrupole mass filter**, the opposite pairs of the four rods carry a voltage U + V cos ωt and −(U + V cos ωt). For a given U and V, the paths of ions of only one m/z are stable and pass through the rods; the others strike a rod and are lost. Scanning U and V (keeping U/V constant) scans the mass. It is a filter (and not a storage device), so it is inherently a scanning instrument: when it scans 1000 m/z values, it spends only 0.1% of the time on each, which costs sensitivity. Setting it to a single m/z (SIM) restores the sensitivity.

In **time-of-flight**, all ions get the same kinetic energy zeU = ½mv², so the velocity is v = (2zeU/m)^{1/2} and the flight time over a path L is t = L(m/2zeU)^{1/2}: t² ∝ m/z. A **reflectron** (an ion mirror) compensates for the spread of initial energies, and doubles the path in a compact instrument, and increases the resolving power from 10³ to 2 × 10⁴ or more. A whole spectrum is recorded in each pulse, so a TOF is the natural detector for fast chromatography and for pulsed sources.

Atomic masses are not integers (¹²C is 12.00000 by definition, but ¹H is 1.007825, ¹⁶O 15.994915, ¹⁴N 14.003074), and the difference from the integer mass is the **mass defect**. Two ions of the same nominal mass but a different composition have a slightly different exact mass, and a high-resolution instrument separates them and identifies the elemental formula from the measured exact mass.

example.title: Resolving N₂ from CO
example.problem: N₂⁺• and CO⁺• both have nominal mass 28. What resolving power separates them, and what do ppm mass error limits do for assigning formulas?
example.solution: N₂ = 2 × 14.003074 = 28.006148. CO = 12.000000 + 15.994915 = 27.994915. Δm = 0.011233. R = 28/0.0112 ≈ 2500. This needs a TOF or Orbitrap, and cannot be done by a unit-resolution quadrupole. For formula assignment, at m/z 300 a 3 ppm error is ±0.0009 u, which usually leaves only one or two formulas of C, H, N and O consistent with the measured mass, and the isotope pattern removes the remainder.

sections.title: Tandem mass spectrometry
body: In **tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS)** one mass analyzer selects an ion (the **precursor ion**), a collision cell fragments it, and a second analyzer measures the fragments (**product ions**). In **collision-induced dissociation (CID)** the selected ions are accelerated into a cell with 10⁻³–10⁻² mbar of argon or nitrogen; the collisions convert kinetic energy into internal energy, and the ions fragment by the weakest bonds. Because the fragments come from one chosen ion, the spectrum of a component can be obtained from a mixture without a prior separation, and gives the structure (peptide sequencing, drug metabolite identification).
The **triple quadrupole** is the workhorse of quantitative analysis: Q1 (mass filter) – q2 (the collision cell, an RF-only quadrupole) – Q3 (mass filter). Its scan modes are:

list: **Product ion scan**: Q1 fixed on the precursor, Q3 scans. Gives the structure of a selected ion.
**Precursor ion scan**: Q3 fixed on a diagnostic fragment, Q1 scans. Finds all the compounds that give this fragment (e.g. all glucuronides, m/z 113).
**Neutral loss scan**: Q1 and Q3 scan together with a fixed mass offset (e.g. 98 u for the loss of H₃PO₄ from phosphopeptides).

**Selected/multiple reaction monitoring (SRM/MRM)**: Q1 and Q3 both fixed on a chosen precursor → product pair (a *transition*). Only the analyte that has the right precursor mass and gives the right fragment is detected, so the chemical noise is greatly reduced, and the sensitivity (pg to fg) and the selectivity are the best of any MS mode. One quantifier transition and a second qualifier transition (the ratio of the two must match a standard) are monitored for each compound, with dozens of compounds per run.

body: Hybrid instruments combine the advantages: the **Q-TOF** (a quadrupole for selection, a collision cell, a TOF for high-resolution product ions) and the Orbitrap hybrids give accurate masses of precursors and fragments. Ion traps can repeat the cycle: isolate, fragment, isolate a fragment, fragment (MSⁿ), which is useful for the structures of glycans and natural products.

example.title: An MRM method
example.problem: Caffeine ([M+H]⁺ = m/z 195) fragments mainly to m/z 138 (loss of 57, CH₃NCO) and 110. Write the SRM method, and why use two transitions?
example.solution: Quantifier: 195 → 138 (the strongest). Qualifier: 195 → 110. Q1 is fixed at 195, Q3 alternates between 138 and 110, each for a dwell time of 20–50 ms. Another compound with the same precursor mass (isobaric) is unlikely to give both fragments in the same ratio, so the qualifier/quantifier ratio (within ±20% of the standard) confirms identity, and the signal at 138 is used for the calibration.

sections.title: GC–MS
body: In **GC–MS** the effluent of a capillary column (1–2 mL min⁻¹ of helium) flows directly into the EI source, since the vacuum system of the instrument takes this flow rate. The column’s separation (see the chapter on chromatography) and the spectrum’s identification together make the most widely used method for volatile and semi-volatile organic compounds: environmental pollutants, drugs and metabolites (after derivatization), flavors, petroleum, forensic samples.

list: In **full-scan** mode the quadrupole scans, for example, m/z 40–500 every 0.2 s, giving a mass spectrum at every point in the chromatogram. The sum of all ion intensities at each time is the **total ion chromatogram (TIC)**. A mass spectrum of a peak is compared with a **spectral library** (the NIST library): a search gives a ranked list of matches with a match factor. A match above ~800/1000 is a likely identification, but it must be confirmed by the retention index or a standard because isomers have almost identical spectra.
An **extracted ion chromatogram (XIC)** plots one m/z against time. It finds a compound in a crowded TIC by its characteristic ion (m/z 149 for phthalates, m/z 91 for alkylbenzenes).

In **selected ion monitoring (SIM)** the quadrupole jumps between 2–5 chosen ions and spends the whole time on them. The sensitivity increases 10–100 times with respect to full scan, so SIM is used for target compounds at trace levels (dioxins, pesticides), at the price of the library search.

The instrument is tuned with a calibrant, **perfluorotributylamine (PFTBA)**, which gives fragments at m/z 69, 219 and 502 across the mass range, used to adjust the lens voltages and the mass axis, and to check the relative abundances.

body: The isotope pattern in an EI spectrum shows the composition: a chlorine-containing ion shows M and M+2 with the ratio 3:1 (³⁵Cl:³⁷Cl), a compound with Br shows M and M+2 at 1:1, and the M+1 peak (1.1% per carbon) gives the number of carbons. These are discussed in the organic spectroscopy chapter.

example.title: SIM versus full scan
example.problem: A GC–MS method to measure benzo[a]pyrene (m/z 252) in smoked food has an LOD of 5 µg kg⁻¹ in full scan. Why is SIM better, and which ions are monitored?
example.solution: In SIM the instrument measures only m/z 252 (quantifier), 253 and 250 (qualifiers) with a dwell time of about 100 ms each, instead of scanning 450 masses. The time on the analyte ion increases by a factor of about 100–1000, so the S/N improves by about 10–30× and LOD falls to 0.1–0.5 µg kg⁻¹. The qualifier ratios (253/252 ≈ 22%, from ¹³C, and 250/252 ≈ 25%, from the loss of H₂) confirm identity.

sections.title: LC–MS and quantitation
body: **LC–MS** couples a liquid chromatograph to an atmospheric-pressure source (ESI or APCI), which solves the problem of removing 0.2–1 mL min⁻¹ of liquid before the vacuum. It reaches non-volatile, polar, thermally labile and high-mass analytes that GC cannot: drugs and metabolites in plasma, pesticides, peptides, proteins. Triple-quadrupole **LC–MS/MS** in MRM mode is the dominant method for quantitation in complex biological matrices at ng mL⁻¹ and below.

list: **Mobile phase compatibility**: only volatile buffers (ammonium formate or acetate, formic acid at 0.1%) can be used; phosphate buffers and non-volatile salts deposit in the source. Additives in the eluent determine the ions: formic acid favors [M+H]⁺, ammonia or ammonium acetate favor [M−H]⁻, and sodium contamination gives [M+Na]⁺ adducts, which fragment poorly.

**Ion suppression**: the co-eluting matrix components compete with the analyte for the limited charge on the droplet surface and for evaporation, so the response in the sample is lower (or higher) than in solvent. It is not seen in the chromatogram, so it needs to be tested, for example by **post-column infusion** of the analyte while injecting a blank matrix extract and looking for dips in the baseline at the retention time. It is reduced by better sample cleanup (SPE), better chromatographic separation of the analyte from the matrix interferences, dilution, or lower flow rates (nano-ESI).

The most reliable correction is a **stable isotope-labeled internal standard** (e.g. ¹³C₆- or D₅-analogue of the analyte), added at the start of sample preparation. It has the same retention time, extraction recovery and ionization behavior, so it is suppressed to the same extent, and the ratio of the analyte and standard signals remains accurate. This is isotope dilution (see the chapter on quantitative analysis for internal standards).

example.title: Ion suppression
example.problem: A drug at 50 ng mL⁻¹ gives a peak area of 100,000 in methanol, but 55,000 when spiked into plasma extract. Calculate the matrix effect, and the area ratio when a deuterated standard is used and gives areas of 200,000 in solvent and 110,000 in plasma.
example.solution: Matrix effect = 55,000/100,000 = 55%, which is 45% suppression. For the deuterated standard 110,000/200,000 = 55% as well, so the ratio of analyte to standard is 55,000/110,000 = 0.50 in plasma against 100,000/200,000 = 0.50 in solvent. The ratio is not changed, and the quantitation is correct.

It reacts with the column
It raises the pH too far

sections.title: Hyphenated techniques and speciation
body: The total concentration of an element often says little about its risk. Arsenic as inorganic arsenite As(III) is highly toxic, as arsenate As(V) toxic, but as the arsenobetaine in fish it is nearly harmless; mercury as methylmercury accumulates in fish and damages the nervous system, whereas inorganic Hg²⁺ is much less bioavailable; Cr(VI) is carcinogenic and Cr(III) is a nutrient. **Speciation analysis** determines the concentration of each chemical form.

A **hyphenated technique** couples a separation method to an element-specific detector. The species are separated chromatographically, and the ICP-MS then detects the element in each peak, with its high sensitivity, wide dynamic range and an element-selective response that does not depend on the molecular structure of the species (so one calibration with any species of the element gives roughly the response of all).

list: **HPLC–ICP–MS** for arsenic: anion-exchange chromatography with an ammonium carbonate or phosphate eluent, in about 10 minutes, separates arsenobetaine, As(III), dimethylarsinic acid (DMA), monomethylarsonic acid (MMA) and As(V). The column effluent goes straight to the nebulizer, and ⁷⁵As (with the collision cell for ArCl) is monitored. Rice and seafood are standard applications.
**GC–ICP–MS** or GC–AFS with hydride or ethylation derivatization for volatile organometallic species (methylmercury, butyltins).
**IC–ICP–MS** for Cr(III)/Cr(VI) and for iodine species (iodide/iodate), and **CE–ICP–MS** for small samples.

body: Two problems must be controlled: the species must not change during sampling, storage and extraction (e.g. As(III) oxidizes, Hg is methylated or lost), and quantitation needs a certified reference material for the species, or species-specific isotope dilution, in which an enriched-isotope-labeled form of each species is added to the sample.

example.title: Total vs species
example.problem: Rice contains total arsenic of 0.30 mg kg⁻¹ by ICP-MS. HPLC–ICP–MS finds 0.12 inorganic As (As(III) + As(V)), 0.15 DMA, 0.03 MMA. Why does the species result matter?
example.solution: The sum of the species is 0.30 mg kg⁻¹, so recovery of the total is 100%. Regulations on rice (for example a Codex limit of 0.2 mg kg⁻¹ for polished rice) apply to the inorganic arsenic, the species of greatest toxicity. Here 0.12 mg kg⁻¹ is below the limit, although the total is above it; a total-arsenic measurement would have condemned acceptable rice.

check.q: Why does ICP-MS detection suit speciation after HPLC?
check.a: It gives element-specific, sensitive detection of each separated species
wrong: It gives structural information of each species
It separates the species itself
It avoids the need for chromatography

quiz.q: A protein of mass 20,000 u forms the ion [M+10H]¹⁰⁺ in ESI. At what m/z does it appear (proton mass 1.00728 u)?
quiz.why: m/z = (M + n × 1.00728)/n = (20,000 + 10.07)/10 = 2001.0. Adding the protons after dividing by n gives 2010.1, and ignoring them gives 2000.0, which is not the value that a high-resolution measurement would see.

quiz.q: A moderately nonpolar pesticide of medium mass is poorly ionized by ESI because it carries no charge in solution. Which LC-compatible source is the better choice?
quiz.a: APCI, in which corona-generated solvent ions protonate the analyte
wrong: EI, since it ionizes any compound present in the LC effluent in the vacuum
MALDI, since it can ionize neutral molecules with a laser pulse and a matrix
ESI at a higher capillary voltage, which charges neutral molecules directly
quiz.why: APCI ionizes in the gas phase after the heated nebulizer evaporates the eluent, so the analyte does not need to be a preformed ion in solution. EI needs a gas-phase sample in vacuum, so it cannot take LC effluent directly.

quiz.q: A volatile compound shows no molecular ion in its 70 eV EI spectrum. How can its molar mass be found with the same GC–MS instrument?
quiz.a: Switch to chemical ionization, which gives mainly [M+H]⁺
wrong: Raise the electron energy so that the molecule survives
Search the EI spectrum against the NIST library
Switch to a MALDI matrix and a TOF analyzer
quiz.why: In CI a reagent gas such as CH₄ transfers a proton gently, leaving little internal energy for fragmentation. More electron energy would deposit more energy and fragment the ion further.

quiz.q: Why is MALDI normally paired with a time-of-flight analyzer?
quiz.a: Laser pulses give ions in bursts, which defines the start time for TOF
wrong: MALDI ions are always multiply charged and need the large mass range of TOF
MALDI generates a continuous ion beam that only TOF can sample efficiently
TOF is the only analyzer that tolerates the matrix crystals in the source
quiz.why: TOF measures the time from a start pulse to arrival, so a pulsed source suits it well. MALDI gives mostly singly charged ions, and the large mass range of TOF is a further advantage.

quiz.q: Two ions at m/z 400.000 and 400.016 must just be resolved. What resolving power is needed?
quiz.why: R = m/Δm = 400/0.016 = 25,000. This is reached by a good reflectron TOF or Orbitrap but not by a unit-resolution quadrupole.

quiz.q: An Orbitrap gives m/z 301.1412 for an ion whose calculated m/z is 301.1416. What is the mass error?
wrong: +1.3 ppm
−13 ppm
−0.4 ppm
quiz.why: Error = (301.1412 − 301.1416)/301.1416 × 10⁶ = −1.3 ppm. The measured value is below the true value, so the sign is negative; −0.4 is the error in u×10³ rather than ppm.

quiz.q: Two singly charged ions are accelerated through the same voltage in a TOF analyzer, and one is 4 times heavier. How do their flight times compare?
quiz.a: The heavier ion takes twice as long
wrong: The heavier ion takes 4 times as long
The heavier ion takes 16 times as long
The heavier ion arrives first, because it carries more momentum
quiz.why: All ions get the same kinetic energy, so v ∝ (1/m)^½ and t ∝ m^½. A fourfold mass gives a twofold longer flight time, and lighter ions always arrive first.

quiz.q: Which instrument can confirm an elemental formula in a complex mixture from an exact mass to within 1 ppm?
wrong: A triple quadrupole
A linear ion trap
A single quadrupole in SIM mode
quiz.why: Orbitraps and FT-ICR instruments combine resolving power of 10⁵–10⁷ with sub-ppm to low-ppm accuracy. Quadrupoles and ion traps work at unit resolution with errors of hundreds of ppm.

quiz.q: A triple quadrupole runs a neutral loss scan for the loss of 98 u from singly charged phosphopeptides. When Q1 transmits m/z 800, where is Q3 set?
wrong: m/z 98
quiz.why: Q1 and Q3 scan together with a fixed offset, and the fragment is the precursor minus the neutral: 800 − 98 = 702. The value 898 adds the loss instead of subtracting it.

quiz.q: In an MRM method the qualifier/quantifier ratio of a standard is 0.25, with a tolerance of ±20% (relative). A sample peak gives 0.45. What does this indicate?
quiz.a: Not confirmed: an interferent probably contributes to one transition
wrong: The identity is confirmed, since both transitions are present at the right retention time
The identity is confirmed, but the concentration must exceed that of the standard
The method has lost sensitivity and the instrument must be recalibrated
quiz.why: The acceptable range is 0.20–0.30, so 0.45 lies outside it. A true analyte fragments in a fixed ratio, so a different ratio shows that something else is contributing to one of the channels.

quiz.q: Why can an ion trap perform MS³ while a triple quadrupole cannot?
quiz.a: A trap repeats isolation and CID in time, a triple quadrupole has fixed stages in space
wrong: A triple quadrupole cannot fragment ions at all, since it has no collision cell
A trap uses higher collision energies, which allows two fragmentation steps in one run
A trap has a higher resolving power, so a fragment can be selected a second time
quiz.why: In Q1–q2–Q3 each step has its own hardware, so there is one fragmentation only. Confining ions in a trap lets the cycle of isolation and CID be repeated (MSⁿ).

quiz.q: A quadrupole scans 500 m/z units in each cycle. In SIM mode it monitors 2 ions in the same cycle time. By what factor does the time spent on each ion increase?
quiz.why: Scanning spends 1/500 of the cycle on each mass, SIM 1/2, so the dwell time per ion rises by 500/2 = 250. This is why SIM is 10–100 times more sensitive, at the cost of a library-searchable spectrum.

quiz.q: A GC–MS library search gives 1,2-dimethylbenzene as the top hit, with a match factor of 920/1000. Why should this not be reported on its own?
quiz.a: Isomers such as the xylenes give nearly identical EI spectra, so the retention index or a standard is needed
wrong: Match factors above 800 are never reliable
EI spectra of aromatic compounds change from one instrument to another
Aromatic compounds do not give a molecular ion in EI
quiz.why: A high match factor means a similar spectrum, not a unique one, and positional isomers fragment in almost the same way. Retention time on the column is what tells them apart.

quiz.q: Which eluent additive best promotes [M+H]⁺ ions for positive-mode LC–ESI-MS?
wrong: 20 mM sodium phosphate
0.1% aqueous ammonia
10 mM sodium chloride
quiz.why: Formic acid is volatile and supplies protons. Sodium phosphate fouls the source, ammonia favors [M−H]⁻, and sodium salts give [M+Na]⁺ adducts that fragment poorly.

quiz.q: An analyte gives an area of 90,000 in solvent and 63,000 when spiked into plasma extract. What is the matrix effect (response in plasma as a percentage of that in solvent)?
quiz.why: 63,000/90,000 = 70%, which means 30% ion suppression. Reporting 30% mixes up the loss with the response that remains.

quiz.q: During post-column infusion of an analyte, a blank plasma extract is injected and the signal dips at 3.2 min. What does this show?
quiz.a: Matrix components eluting at 3.2 min suppress ionization, so an analyte eluting then would be suppressed
wrong: The analyte elutes from the column at 3.2 min
The detector is saturated by the infused analyte
The column is bleeding stationary phase into the source
quiz.why: The infused analyte gives a constant signal, so a dip means that whatever elutes from the blank at that moment competes for charge. The test locates the suppression zone, which can then be avoided chromatographically.

quiz.q: A rice extract for arsenic speciation is stored warm for several days. The As(III) result falls and As(V) rises. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.a: As(III) is oxidized during storage, so the species has changed
wrong: The ICP-MS responds more strongly to As(V) than to As(III) in the plasma
Arsenate coelutes with arsenobetaine and is counted twice in the integration
The anion-exchange column converts As(III) to As(V) during the separation
quiz.why: Species may interconvert during sampling, storage and extraction, and As(III) is easily oxidized. The ICP-MS response is the same for all arsenic species, so the shift is chemical.

quiz.q: In HPLC–ICP–MS speciation of arsenic, why can a standard of one arsenic species roughly calibrate the others?
quiz.a: The plasma atomizes all species, so the response depends on the arsenic atoms and not on the molecular structure
wrong: All arsenic species elute as one peak from the anion-exchange column
The column converts every species to the same arsenic compound before detection
The quadrupole selects the intact molecular ion of each species
quiz.why: In the 6000–10,000 K plasma the molecule is destroyed and only ⁷⁵As⁺ is counted. This element-selective response is what makes ICP-MS a convenient detector after separation.

summary: Hard sources (EI) fragment molecules, which gives library-searchable spectra. Soft sources (CI, ESI, APCI, MALDI) give the intact ion for molar mass. ESI gives multiply charged ions for large molecules.

Analyzers: quadrupole (unit resolution, robust, SIM/MRM), TOF (unlimited mass range, fast), ion trap (MSⁿ), Orbitrap and FT-ICR (R up to 10⁶–10⁷, ppm accuracy). Resolving power is R = m/Δm; exact masses identify formulas.
MS/MS: select a precursor, fragment it by CID, measure the products. Triple quadrupole modes: product ion, precursor ion, neutral loss and SRM/MRM, the most selective and sensitive quantitation mode.
GC–MS: EI, library search, TIC, XIC, SIM for trace analysis. LC–MS: volatile buffers, ion suppression, stable isotope-labeled internal standards.
Speciation: HPLC–ICP–MS and similar hyphenated methods quantify the toxic forms of an element rather than only its total concentration.

problems.q: What resolving power is needed to separate C₂H₄⁺• (28.0313) from N₂⁺• (28.0061) and from CO⁺• (27.9949)? Which analyzers can do it?
problems.solution: Smallest gap: C₂H₄/N₂: Δm = 0.0252, R = 28/0.0252 ≈ 1100 (a good quadrupole or any TOF). N₂/CO: Δm = 0.0112, R ≈ 2500 (TOF, Orbitrap, FT-ICR). C₂H₄ to CO: Δm = 0.0364, R ≈ 770. So R ≥ 2500 resolves all three: a TOF with reflectron, Orbitrap or FT-ICR; not a unit-resolution quadrupole.
problems.a: About 2500 for all three; TOF, Orbitrap or FT-ICR.

problems.q: An Orbitrap measures a peak at m/z 609.2812 for a compound with formula C₃₃H₄₀N₂O₉ (in its protonated form, calculated m/z 609.2807). Compute the mass error.
problems.solution: Error = (609.2812 − 609.2807)/609.2807 × 10⁶ = 0.0005/609.28 × 10⁶ = 0.8 ppm. This is within the 1–3 ppm typical of the Orbitrap, so the formula is consistent.

problems.q: A TOF analyzer has a 1.00 m flight tube and accelerates singly charged ions through 20.0 kV. Calculate the flight time of an ion of m = 1000 u. (1 u = 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)
Explain why a triple quadrupole in MRM mode can detect a drug in plasma at 1 ng mL⁻¹ while a single quadrupole in SIM mode cannot do so reliably.
problems.solution: In SIM, any co-eluting plasma component that has an ion at the same m/z contributes to the signal (chemical noise). In MRM, the interference must have the same precursor mass and also give the same fragment, which is much less likely, so the background is reduced by a factor of 10–1000, and the S/N rises by the same factor even if the absolute signal of the analyte is a little lower.
problems.a: Two stages of mass selection remove chemical noise from the matrix.
